newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia Budget-Access sees A$2.6 bln start point.
newsitem.headline: Australia Budget-Access sees A$2.6 bln start point.

text.p: Australian government finances are in better condition that shown in official estimates and the 1997/98 budget deficit to be announced next week should be lower than expected, forecasters Access Economics said on Wednesday.

Access, which produces Australia's most detailed private fiscal estimates, said in its annual budget preview that the 1997/98 underlying deficit would be no more than A$2.6 billion even before Treasurer Peter Costello implements further cuts in the May 13 budget.

The latest government budget estimates, issued in January, said current fiscal policies would produce an underlying deficit -- that is, excluding asset sales -- of A$3.9 billion for the year to June 1998 and A$2.2 billion for the following year.
Access said its forecasts were different to the government's because the government assumed continuous 3.5 percent economic growth, whereas Access saw a rising rate of growth.

Access budget analyst Chris Richardson told Reuters that data issued since he finalised his estimates, particularly wages and the latest government financial statistics, suggested the 1997/98 budget starting point might be even lower than A$2.6 billion.
The current fiscal year's deficit would be A$7.7 billion or lower, not the A$8.5 billion that the government projected in its latest forecasts in January, Richardson said.
And the 1998/99 budget balance, which the government projects at a A$2.2 billion deficit, will be a surplus of A$2.5 billion.
(An accompanying report tabulates Access's forecasts in detail.)
Access sees a radically stronger overall or "headline" budget balance in 1996/97, thanks to unbudgeted money from asset sales and a special dividend from telecoms carrier Telstra Corp.

While Telstra says it will deposit an unbudgeted A$3 billion into the Treasury by the end of the year, the government is expected later on Wednesday to announce proceeds from airport proceeds much greater than the budgeted A$1.5 billion or so.
With this extra money, the 1996/97 headline budget balance should be a surplus of A$3.4 billion, not the A$2.7 billion deficit projected in the mid-year review.
The government's current fiscal target is to eliminate the deficit for 1998/99. According to Access, it will not have to lift a finger to do so -- the budget is heading into surplus on its own.
"For bond markets, it implies a supply driven fall in yields compared to where they would otherwise have been," Access said.

The government has marked down its fiscal forecasts three times since it took office -- once just after the March 1996 election win, again in the August 1996 budget and a third time in the January mid-year review.
